1.pericope_label: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven... I have seen the travail, which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it

schools.summary: Delitzsch separates the two Hebrew words for time into a predetermined span and a season suited to the matter, approves the Greek rendering by chronos and kairos, refuses to soften killing into wounding, and insists the catalogue is not arranged on moral grounds; Ellicott dates both key words to later Hebrew and agrees with him that gathering stones is a matter of clearing a field.

Gill takes the season for a fixed moment with a fixed duration and applies it first to the world, which neither existed from everlasting nor arose from a chance concourse of atoms; he reads the stones of the fifth verse as the ruined temple and the gathering of the Gentiles, and holds that a man can promise himself nothing here that will profit him hereafter.

Clarke draws two morals before touching the list — that neglecting an appointed season makes a man the author of his own distresses, and that man alone spends time on ends for which no time was made — observes that only birth and death lie wholly outside human choice, and renders the whole catalogue as blank verse; Wesley adds the qualification that the verse speaks of a time in which things are actually done, not one in which they may lawfully be done.

Henry frames the chapter as a world of changes in which the right posture is an even mind, counts the particulars at twenty-eight after the days of the moon's revolution, and turns the travail of the tenth verse into a gift given as a physician gives medicine.

debates.question: What kind of time is meant?

positions.view: Two things at once: a predetermined point with its duration, and a season appropriate to the matter — the distinction the Greek caught with chronos and kairos.
A time fixed by God in which things are actually done, and expressly not a time allowed by God in which they may lawfully be done.
A season a man may keep or neglect, so that whoever misses it sins against providence and authors his own distress.
A set moment together with a set duration, fixed for the world itself as much as for anything in it.

debates.question: What lies behind the casting and gathering of stones?

positions.view: Agriculture: stones thrown into a field spoil it, stones gathered out bring it under cultivation.
The ruined temple and the gathering of the Gentiles, with the casting away and recovery of the Jews.
Fortification: demolishing strongholds when God gives peace, and raising them when war returns.

outliers.note: Observes that the list gives a time to be born and a time to die but no time to live, life being too short to be worth the mention, and that weeping is placed before laughing because we must first sow in tears.
Sets the whole catalogue in blank verse, and reports that Jewish readers find their nation's history in these pairs while others find the fortunes of the church.

themes: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace.
What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth?
I have seen the travail, which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it.

11.pericope_label: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart... God requireth that which is past

schools.summary: Delitzsch weighs the moral and the eudemonistic senses of the twelfth verse and leaves the difficulty standing, reads the fourteenth as a conclusion from experience valid for the future as well as the present, and renders the last clause of the fifteenth as God seeking what has been crowded out, against the version that makes it God seeking the persecuted; Ellicott argues on lexical grounds that the disputed noun of the eleventh verse means eternity rather than world, and takes the fifteenth as recalling the past rather than judging it.

Gill distinguishes what God does immediately, what he does through instruments and what he merely permits, finding harmony in all three, and reads the eating and drinking as moderate, cheerful and shared with the poor.

Clarke takes the noun for eternity and turns the clause positive, holding that God has rooted eternity in every heart, and presses the permanence of God's work into the claim that nothing made will finally be destroyed and no new order of beings produced; Wesley defends providence against shallow judgment and limits man's capacity to read the world, some works remaining past finding out.

Henry insists that what seems most unpleasant is becoming in its own season, compares our position to that of onlookers at a picture still being drawn, and reports the two opposite constructions of the world set in men's hearts, as a capacity to read providence or as an impediment to reading it.

debates.question: What has God set in the heart?

positions.view: Eternity; the noun means world only in post-biblical Hebrew, and read as eternity it explains why a man longing for permanence cannot make out the work God does.
Eternity, taken positively: the idea is rooted in every heart, and without it a man could not trace the divine work at all.
The world, understood as a capacity to read providence which God has given men.
The world, in both senses at once: some make it the reason we might know more of God's works, others the reason we know less.

debates.question: Does the twelfth verse counsel doing good or enjoying good?

positions.view: Enjoyment; the moral rendering is nowhere else given to this conclusion, and the following verse assumes it — though no parallel exists for the phrase meaning to be of good cheer either.
Enjoyment, though the phrase is elsewhere always moral; the context requires it here.
Both: use what God gives without harming yourself, and spend it in charity toward others.

outliers.note: Extends the permanence of God's work into a doctrine of universal indestructibility — no being God has made will be annihilated, the brute creation restored and every human spirit living for ever — and turns the closing clause on the reader, asking where the earlier stirrings of the Spirit have gone.
Answers the objection from the ugliness of particular seasons with the observation that night in its turn is a black beauty as day is a bright one.

themes: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life.
And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God.
I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him.
That which hath been is now; and that which is to be hath already been; and God requireth that which is past.

16.pericope_label: And moreover I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there... a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity

schools.summary: Delitzsch notes the palindromic construction of the sixteenth verse, finds a double sense in the verb of the seventeenth because the righteous are named first, derives the disputed infinitive of the eighteenth from a root of cutting and renders it that God might sift them, and settles the pointing of the nineteenth by manuscript evidence; Ellicott names the theme as the imperfection of moral retribution in this life, and insists the judgment of the seventeenth verse is offered as a belief in conflict with the doubts following, not as a settled conclusion.

Gill identifies the corrupt courts with the Jewish tribunals after the older rabbinic reading, rests on a judgment to come known from reason, tradition and scripture, and rejects the proposal that the wise man is impersonating the atheist and the epicure in the verses about the beasts.

Clarke casts his comment on the corrupt tribunal as verse, gives the later judgment an epigram, adopts a translation turning the eighteenth verse into a wish for enlightenment and refers it to the corrupt magistrates rather than to mankind, and notes that animal life is identical in man and beast; Wesley reads the judgment as consolation reached after grief and adds that men have made themselves beasts by their practices.

Henry supplies the indignation the passage needs, that a judge without the fear of God turns a refuge into a prison for oppressed innocence, and that it were better such a people had no judges and such judges no power.

debates.question: How firmly is the judgment to come asserted?

positions.view: Not firmly: it is a belief in conflict with the doubts that follow, and the repeated formula conveys no more than I thought, and then again I thought.
As a certainty known from reason, tradition and scripture, which relieved the writer under the perversion of justice.
As a fixed appointment which must be waited for, the verb covering both vindication and sentence.
As a settled expectation: man has his time below and God his above.

debates.question: Whose voice speaks in the comparison with the beasts?

positions.view: The writer's own; the reading that makes him quote the language of ordinary men, or record the thoughts of the unwise, is to be rejected.
The writer's, as a wish rather than a statement — that God would enlighten them — and directed at the corrupt magistrates, not at mankind.
The writer's, as a description of what men have made of themselves, true only in respect of the present life.

outliers.note: Records that the clause about what befalls the beasts is wanting in six of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi.

Presses the office rather than the man: a judge ruled by religion is God's own deputy, one of those to whom it is said, You are gods, so that corruption in the seat makes the office not merely vain but a lie.

themes: And moreover I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there; and the place of righteousness, that iniquity was there.
I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.
I said in mine heart concerning the estate of the sons of men, that God might manifest them, and that they might see that they themselves are beasts.

For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity.

20.pericope_label: All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again... for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the one place as the earth and distinguishes the generic from the retrospective article, then makes the whole difficulty explicit — it remains possible that the spirit of a dying man differs from that of a dying beast, and that is exactly what is in question; he rejects on three grounds the construction that turns the twenty-first verse from a question into a statement, and answers a proposal to read the closing clause of the chapter as concerning the state of the world after a man's death. Ellicott follows the Greek and the majority in reading the verse as a doubt, and states the sceptical thought plainly.

Gill grants that men and beasts share one breath and denies that they share one spirit, since a man's soul is rational and immortal and returns at death to God; on the last verse he notes a paraphrase that makes the man rejoice in his good works, taken as vindication before men rather than justification before God.

Clarke turns the common grave into verse, offers his own translation in which the two clauses of the twenty-first verse become assertions rather than questions, observes that the same Hebrew word meant breath in the previous verse and means spirit here, and ends in exhortation; Wesley allows the difference between the two spirits but observes that most people never attend to it.

debates.question: Is the twenty-first verse a question or a statement?

positions.view: A sceptical question; every ancient translator read the particles as interrogative, the formula who knoweth leads one to expect it, and the connection requires a doubt.
A statement of real difference: the spirit of man is rational and immortal and goes upward to God, whatever breath he shares with the beast.
A statement, to be rendered as assertions — the immortal spirit of the sons of Adam ascending, the breath of the cattle going down to the earth.
A real difference which good men know and most people ignore, their hearts being set on what is present and visible.

outliers.note: States the problem the chapter leaves open rather than resolving it, allowing that the spirit of a dying man may differ from that of a dying beast while insisting that this is precisely what cannot be known.
Leaves exegesis for exhortation at the close, urging the reader not to turn God's blessings into sin by complaining, since a man wretched without may still be happy within.

themes: All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?
Wherefore I perceive that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?
